domain_title: Community Prosperity Accounts — Local Equity in Places People Build
research_domain_title: Community Equity, Community Investment Units, Civic Equity Credits, and Local Capital Formation
note: Major dedicated architecture elaborating Prosperous Aging Layer 3 (Local Community Prosperity Accounts / Trusts) and linking Civic Wealth contribution pathways to place-based ownership. Complements — does not replace — diversified national/international retirement savings. Illustrative local allocation band (e.g., 5–20%) requires modeling. Legal drafting 0%. Architecture ≠ evidence that Community Investment Units or Community Prosperity Funds already exist as described.

core_question.text: What if citizens could become long-term investors in the prosperity of the communities they help build?

core_principle.text: Communities create wealth through infrastructure, education, entrepreneurship, public safety, housing, healthcare, parks, transportation, utilities, tourism, and civic trust — yet citizens who spend decades building those assets rarely own part of the increase in value. The goal is community equity, not simply another pension.

compact_language.text: Every American should have the opportunity to own a stake in the long-term prosperity of the community they help build. Communities should be able to raise capital from their own residents for productive public investments, allowing citizens to share in the wealth created by stronger schools, modern infrastructure, successful local businesses, and responsible stewardship. Community ownership should complement—not replace—diversified retirement savings, aligning personal financial security with the enduring success of the places people call home.

foundational_communities_bridge.text: Community Prosperity Accounts reinforce foundational communities: longer-term investment in educating local citizens, improving energy and essential infrastructure, and making places more valuable so businesses and families choose to stay and arrive — circulating prosperity where people live.

two_retirement_components.summary: Every citizen can have two complementary retirement components.

traditional_retirement.title: Traditional Retirement
traditional_retirement.text: Diversified national and international investments protect against local downturns and remain the majority of retirement capital.

community_prosperity_account.title: Community Prosperity Account
community_prosperity_account.text: A smaller share — for example an illustrative 5–20% band, potentially chosen by the individual — may be invested in approved local productive projects. Exact percentages require modeling and fiduciary caps.
example_assets: municipal solar and community energy systems
food processing facilities and public markets

community_investment_units.title: Community Investment Units
community_investment_units.summary: Instead of issuing only municipal bonds to outside investors, cities and regions may create Community Investment Units that residents purchase — or receive through verified participation — to finance productive infrastructure. As projects generate revenue, returns flow to citizen-owners rather than only as interest to distant bondholders.
community_investment_units.design_rule: Units finance productive, revenue-capable or clearly sustainable public-benefit assets under fiduciary rules — not political patronage projects.

incentive_structure.title: A New Incentive Structure
incentive_structure.from: If a new employer comes to town, citizens celebrate but often receive almost nothing directly.
incentive_structure.to: When employment, sales activity, local business, energy production, or downtown value grow in ways that grow the Community Prosperity Fund, investors and participation-credit earners share in that growth.

psychology_shift.from: What can I get from city hall?
psychology_shift.to: How do we help this town succeed?

citizenship_creates_equity.title: Citizenship Creates Equity
citizenship_creates_equity.summary: Ownership is not purchased by dollars alone. Citizens may earn Community Equity Credits for verified contribution, increasing share in the community investment pool under transparent statutory rules.
citizenship_creates_equity.underlying_idea: Civic contribution becomes one pathway — alongside financial investment — to participate in the community’s long-term prosperity.
citizenship_creates_equity.links_to_civic_wealth: Complements Civic Wealth Ladder and Civic Investment Accounts without converting political favor into secret equity.

cities_as_wealth_builders.title: Cities Become Wealth Builders
cities_as_wealth_builders.budget_question: How do we balance next year's budget?
cities_as_wealth_builders.wealth_question: What investments will increase community wealth over the next thirty years?
cities_as_wealth_builders.evaluation_rule: Every major investment is evaluated partly on expected public benefit and financial sustainability.

prosperity_metrics.title: Community Wealth Metrics
prosperity_metrics.summary: Instead of treating GDP alone as the scoreboard, publish Community Wealth metrics that become the 'stock price' of the community.
examples: children staying or returning after college

healthy_competition.title: Healthy Local Competition
healthy_competition.summary: Cities compete on schools, entrepreneurship, family attraction, downtown restoration, public health, and retirement wealth — prosperity becomes measurable.

safeguards.title: Preventing Abuse
safeguards.summary: Institutional design protects participants from political favoritism and imprudent concentration.

rules.text: Community investments complement — not replace — broadly diversified retirement savings so residents are not overly exposed to one local economy.
Investment decisions are made by a professional, fiduciary-governed board rather than elected officials acting alone.
Every project publishes expected costs, risks, projected returns, and ongoing performance.
Regular financial and performance audits are required.
Caps on the percentage of retirement assets invested locally reduce concentration risk. Illustrative bands require modeling.
Participants have clearly defined redemption or transfer rules where appropriate; benefits should vest without permanently trapping people geographically.

political_shift.title: Why This Changes Politics
to_questions: How do we grow the value of our community?
How do we build healthy neighborhoods?
political_shift.outcome: Citizens stop seeing government only as a provider of services and begin seeing themselves as co-owners of a community enterprise.

pillars.title: Dual Retirement Architecture
pillars.summary: Majority diversified traditional retirement plus optional Community Prosperity Account slice.

pillars.title: Community Prosperity Account
pillars.summary: Approved local productive projects with dividends, appreciation, and ownership credits.

pillars.title: Community Investment Units
pillars.summary: Resident capital formation for productive infrastructure alongside — not only instead of — municipal debt.

pillars.title: Community Equity Credits
pillars.summary: Verified civic contribution as a pathway into the community investment pool.

pillars.title: Thirty-Year Wealth Builder Mandate
pillars.summary: Local leaders evaluate investments for long-horizon community wealth, not only annual budgets.

pillars.title: Community Wealth Scoreboard
pillars.summary: Publish household wealth, ownership, education, health, affordability, and retention metrics.

pillars.title: Fiduciary Guardrails
pillars.summary: Diversification, independent boards, transparency, audits, exposure caps, and exit/portability rules.

pillars.title: Co-Owner Civic Culture
pillars.summary: Align personal security with place success so politics asks how to grow community value.

pillars.title: Foundational Community Loop
pillars.summary: Link education, energy, food systems, health, housing, and enterprise so places become more valuable to stay in and move toward.

pillars.title: Shared Prosperity Pathways
pillars.summary: Military, civic, teaching, entrepreneurship, farming, and long-term engagement increase opportunity to participate in community wealth.

items.text: According to the Investment Company Institute (2025 Fact Book quick facts), the U.S. retirement market held about $44.1 trillion at year-end 2024; IRAs ($17.0 trillion) and defined-contribution plans ($12.4 trillion) were about 67% of that total, and mutual funds managed about 45% of those account-based retirement assets — illustrating that retirement savings are heavily pooled in nationally offered fund vehicles rather than place-based ownership stakes.

According to MSRB municipal market materials citing Federal Reserve Financial Accounts data, U.S. municipal capital is raised primarily through municipal securities markets in which holders receive contractual interest and principal — a debt-financing structure, not automatic resident equity ownership of the upside of community projects.

GAO found that about one in ten low-income households approaching retirement (ages 51–64) had a retirement account balance in 2019, compared with about nine in ten high-income households — underscoring unequal access to ownership vehicles that Community Prosperity design must not worsen through imprudent local concentration.

community_prosperity_test.purpose: Questions that keep Community Prosperity design honest.
questions: Does the Community Prosperity Account complement — not replace — diversified retirement savings?
Are local allocation percentages capped and fiduciary-governed rather than politically discretionary?
Do Community Investment Units finance productive assets with published costs, risks, and performance?
Can citizens earn equity through contribution without converting patronage into secret ownership?
Do benefits vest with partial portability so people are not trapped in a failing locality?
Are Community Wealth metrics published so residents can see whether the place is becoming more valuable?
Does the design strengthen education, energy, food, health, and enterprise loops that make communities worth staying in and moving toward?
